vulnerabilities.description: Initializing the DNS stub resolver from an /etc/resolv.conf file, or a LOCALDOMAIN environment variable, whose search list contains a domain of roughly 200 characters or more in the GNU C Library version 2.26 to 2.44 results in an assertion failure which aborts the process. The resolver truncates the search list when copying it into the fixed-size _res.defdname buffer, then asserts that the copy is consistent with the full configuration. The consistency check compared against the wrong size and did not handle a first entry that does not fit, so a correctly truncated list failed the assertion. Any process that resolves names through the library is affected, including long-running processes that reload /etc/resolv.conf on the next query after it changes. Search domains are commonly written to /etc/resolv.conf from data received over DHCP or from a VPN server, so an attacker on the local network may be able to trigger this without privileges on the target system, subject to validation by the network configuration software.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. This image's DNS configuration is not attacker- controlled.

ratings.justification: Requires attacker control of the container's /etc/resolv.conf or LOCALDOMAIN; not a remote trigger.

analysis.detail: glibc DNS stub resolver assertion-abort issue when /etc/resolv.conf or LOCALDOMAIN contains a ~200+ character search-list domain. Requires attacker control of the container's DNS configuration; not remotely triggerable against this image.

vulnerabilities.description: The nscd service in the GNU C Library 2.3.4 onwards may crash due to a stack overflow when a malicious DNS server returns too large a response for a DNS query, resulting in degraded DNS resolution for the system. Exploitation of this bug needs a system that has nscd enabled and using an untrusted DNS server for name resolution, with the compromised DNS server being capable of processing records large enough to result in a stack overflow in an nscd thread stack. During experimentation, bind 9 was unable to handle large records, but that could change in future or with a different name server. In typical installations, nscd is executed in an isolated context as its own user without a shell, due to which any compromise of that service is isolated. There is a remote possibility of nscd cache corruption if an attacker manages to get the stack pointer into a desired point in the heap, potentially resulting in other caches in nscd being overwritten with corrupt data through the stack overflow, until the buggy code path eventually results in a crash. Finally, a crash in nscd may result in performance degradation when resolving names, but it does not result in a denial of service.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. This image does not run nscd.

ratings.justification: This minimal image runs no nscd process; the vulnerable service is absent.

analysis.detail: glibc nscd stack-overflow crash when a malicious DNS server returns an oversized response. Requires nscd running against an untrusted DNS server; this minimal image runs no nscd process at all.

vulnerabilities.description: sha256crypt and sha512crypt through 0.6 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) because the algorithm's runtime is proportional to the square of the length of the password.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. The JVM never calls glibc's crypt() function.

ratings.justification: The JVM never calls glibc's crypt(3); this image performs no local password hashing.

analysis.detail: glibc sha256crypt/sha512crypt algorithmic-complexity denial-of-service issue (CPU cost proportional to the square of password length), which Ubuntu has marked Ignored as architectural (will never be fixed without migrating hash schemes). Affects crypt(3) password hashing, which the JVM never calls.

vulnerabilities.description: A time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to escalate privileges. When expanding $ORIGIN in DT_RPATH for setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs, glibc validates the lexically normalized search path against the trusted directories but then opens the raw, un-normalized path. On systems where fs.protected_hardlinks is disabled, an attacker who hard-links such a program and swaps a path component for a symbolic link can make the loader load an attacker-controlled shared object.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No setuid or setgid binary in the Liquibase Secure image uses $ORIGIN in its search path.

ratings.justification: No setuid or setgid binary in the image carries a $ORIGIN search path, so the vulnerable loader path is never taken.

analysis.detail: Exploitation needs a setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH uses $ORIGIN, plus a local attacker able to hard-link it and win a race. None of the setuid/setgid binaries shipped in the Liquibase Secure image (su, passwd, mount, chsh and the other shadow and util-linux tools) contain $ORIGIN at all, and the container runs Liquibase as the unprivileged liquibase user. fs.protected_hardlinks, enabled by default on major distributions, also blocks the hard-link step.

vulnerabilities.description: A stack-based buffer overflow in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to crash or corrupt the memory of setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs. When such a program's DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN and is followed by NUL or '/', the loader reads past the end of the path buffer and writes past the end of a stack-allocated internal buffer.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No setuid or setgid binary in the Liquibase Secure image uses $ORIGIN in its search path.

ratings.justification: No setuid or setgid binary in the image carries a $ORIGIN search path, so the vulnerable loader path is never taken.

analysis.detail: Exploitation needs a setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN. None of the setuid/setgid binaries shipped in the Liquibase Secure image (su, passwd, mount, chsh and the other shadow and util-linux tools) contain $ORIGIN at all, and the container runs Liquibase as the unprivileged liquibase user.

vulnerabilities.description: The GNU C Library regcomp function from versions 2.4 through 2.41 can double-free memory if an earlier allocation fails, which may permit buffer manipulation depending on the constructed regular expression.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. Liquibase Secure does not call glibc's regcomp() at runtime.

ratings.justification: No process in the Liquibase Secure runtime path compiles regular expressions through glibc, so the vulnerable regcomp() path is never reached.

analysis.detail: libc6 (the glibc shared library itself) is built from the same glibc source package as libc-bin and carries the same version, so the scanner reports it alongside. The same rationale as the libc-bin assessment for this CVE applies: the vulnerable regcomp() double free needs a process that compiles a regular expression through glibc after an earlier allocation failure. An inspection of the shipped image found that neither the JVM nor any JRE native library imports regcomp; Java regular expressions are implemented in java.util.regex, not in glibc. The only importers are OS utilities such as bash, grep, tar and wget, which are either not part of the runtime path or, in the case of the bash entrypoint, do not use regular-expression matching. lpm is a statically linked Go binary.

vulnerabilities.description: Passing an excessively large alignment to memalign, posix_memalign, or aligned_alloc in the GNU C Library can overflow internal arithmetic and lead to heap corruption when the caller controls both the size and the alignment values.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. Liquibase Secure never passes attacker-controlled alignment values to glibc's memalign family.

ratings.justification: The only memalign-family callers in the runtime path pass fixed, runtime-chosen alignments, so the overflow cannot be triggered by attacker input.

analysis.detail: libc6 (the glibc shared library itself) is built from the same glibc source package as libc-bin and carries the same version, so the scanner reports it alongside. The same rationale as the libc-bin assessment for this CVE applies: the vulnerable arithmetic in memalign, posix_memalign and aligned_alloc is triggered only when a caller passes an attacker-controlled, exceptionally large alignment. An inspection of the shipped image found that libjvm.so imports posix_memalign and libmlib_image.so imports memalign, but both pass fixed alignments chosen by the runtime (page and cache-line sizes), never a value derived from user input; no other process in the runtime path uses the memalign family, and lpm is a statically linked Go binary.

vulnerabilities.description: Calling getnetbyaddr or getnetbyaddr_r in the GNU C Library with a configured DNS backend for networks and a zero-valued network query can leak stack contents to the configured DNS resolver.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. Liquibase Secure does not call glibc's getnetbyaddr family at runtime.

ratings.justification: No process in the Liquibase Secure runtime path calls the getnetbyaddr family, and the image's nsswitch.conf has no DNS backend for networks.

analysis.detail: libc6 (the glibc shared library itself) is built from the same glibc source package as libc-bin and carries the same version, so the scanner reports it alongside. The same rationale as the libc-bin assessment for this CVE applies: the stack leak needs a process that calls getnetbyaddr() or getnetbyaddr_r() while nsswitch.conf routes the networks database to DNS. Neither condition holds in the Liquibase Secure image: an inspection found that no JRE native library imports the getnetbyaddr family (the only importers are the getent utility and the perl interpreter, neither of which runs at runtime), and /etc/nsswitch.conf configures networks: files with no dns backend. lpm is a statically linked Go binary.

vulnerabilities.description: Calling wordexp with WRDE_REUSE in conjunction with WRDE_APPEND in the GNU C Library version 2.0 to version 2.42 may cause the interface to return uninitialized memory in the we_wordv member, which on subsequent calls to wordfree may abort the process.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No process in Liquibase Secure calls glibc's wordexp() interface.

ratings.justification: No binary or library in the Liquibase Secure image imports wordexp(), so the vulnerable path is never reached.

analysis.detail: libc6 (the glibc shared library itself) is built from the same glibc source package as libc-bin and carries the same version, so the scanner reports it alongside. The same rationale as the libc-bin assessment for this CVE applies: the uninitialized-memory return needs a process that calls glibc's wordexp() with both WRDE_REUSE and WRDE_APPEND. An inspection of every ELF binary and shared library in the shipped image, including the JRE's native libraries, found none that imports wordexp; the symbol appears only in libc.so.6 itself. lpm is a statically linked Go binary, so the vulnerable wordexp() path is never reached by Liquibase Secure.
